## Statement

Reversing which trial supplies the IPD can reverse the direction of the apparent active-treatment comparison while each analysis remains internally coherent, because the two analyses estimate effects in different target populations. This is not new with Jiang et al. 2025 (doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10), who credit NICE DSU TSD18: Phillippo et al. 2018 (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740) documented the same reversal in a real appraisal, two competing manufacturers' MAICs of secukinumab and adalimumab, and prescribed the remedy this entry proposes, namely deciding which population represents the decision target and transporting the comparison to it under the shared effect modifier assumption. Jiang et al.'s increment is that the paradox persists even when both analyses use the same covariate set. A target-population difference is also not the only way two MAICs can disagree; sampling error, different adjustment sets, model misspecification and measurement differences can each do it.

## Why it is open

Pairwise MAIC contains no mechanism forcing both directions of an analysis to answer the same question, because the target is set by which trial supplies IPD rather than by the decision. The remedy has been on the books since 2018 and has not changed sponsor behavior, since each sponsor's own trial is the natural source of its IPD and nothing obliges two competing submissions to share a target. Transporting both effects to one declared target also needs common support, compatible outcome definitions and enough information to carry both transports, which is often exactly what is missing when the two populations differ enough to produce the reversal. How often the reversal arises and under what covariate configurations is unmeasured, so it is still discovered after submission rather than anticipated.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [Jiang et al. 2025, A critical assessment of matching-adjusted indirect comparisons in relation to target populations, Research Synthesis Methods](https://doi.org/10.1017/rsm.2025.10) | Describes the reversal, its internal coherence and its population explanation, stating that both conclusions are potentially valid within the context of the specific populations considered, and shows the paradox persists with a common covariate set. It credits TSD18 for the original example and recommends IPD sharing rather than ruling on averaging. |
| [Phillippo, Ades, Dias, Palmer, Abrams and Welton 2018, Methods for Population-Adjusted Indirect Comparisons in Health Technology Appraisal, Medical Decision Making (NICE DSU TSD18)](https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X17725740) | Documents the two-way MAIC reversal in practice, with two MAIC analyses from competing manufacturers comparing treatments for ankylosing spondylitis, and prescribes the fix the entry proposes: decide which population represents the decision target and transport the comparison to it under the shared effect modifier assumption. |
| [Fang and He 2026, Arbitrated Indirect Treatment Comparisons](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.18071) | A dedicated methodological response to the MAIC paradox that fixes a single common target, the overlap population, rather than a sponsor-specific one. It does not establish how often the reversal occurs or which target a committee should prefer. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Do not average conflicting MAICs unless the average is deliberately defined as an effect in a specified mixture population and the conditions for that definition hold. The remaining work is empirical and procedural rather than conceptual: characterize how often and under which covariate configurations the reversal arises, and give appraisal committees a rule for what to do when two sponsor submissions target different populations. Fang and He's arbitrated indirect comparison (arxiv:2510.18071) is an existing methodological response that fixes a single common overlap target instead of a sponsor-specific one, so the task is to evaluate it against transporting both effects to an external decision target, not to reinvent it.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.

**The source said.** "Jiang et al. describe a target-population problem in which reversing which trial supplies the IPD can reverse the apparent active-treatment comparison, even when each analysis is internally coherent. The two analyses are not contradictory implementations; they estimate effects in different target populations."

**What was wrong with it.** The source read as though Jiang et al. 2025 discovered the reversal and as though the ban on averaging came from them; the literature auditor found the reversal documented with an applied case in NICE DSU TSD18 nine years earlier (doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740), along with the same prescribed fix, and found no recommendation against averaging in Jiang et al., who instead call for IPD sharing with HTA agencies. GPT-5.6 Sol added that a target-population difference is not the only cause of discordant MAICs and that a weighted average is not invalid in principle if it is deliberately defined as an effect in a specified mixture population.

Literature and prior-art check
:   **partially-solved / supported-with-caveat.** I read the full text of Jiang et al. 2025 (PMC12527493). The reversal, its internal coherence and its population explanation are all verbatim there ('both conclusions ... are potentially valid within the context of the specific populations considered'). But the entry reads as if Jiang et al. discovered the phenomenon. They did not, and they say so, crediting NICE DSU TSD18. Phillippo et al. 2018 Med Decis Making documented the same reversal with a real applied case nine years earlier and prescribed the entry's own proposed direction: 'the real conflict lies not in the different results produced by the 2 MAICs but in deciding which of the 2 study populations better represents the decision target population ... the shared effect modifier assumption, if justified, may be used to transport indirect comparisons into the target population for the decision.' Jiang et al.'s genuine increment is that the paradox persists with the same covariate set. Separately, the claim that averaging is invalid is not in Jiang et al.; they recommend IPD sharing to HTA agencies. Fang & He (arXiv:2510.18071, v2 May 2026) is an explicit methodological response targeting the overlap population.
    Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740: Documents the two-way MAIC reversal in practice and prescribes the fix the entry proposes: declare the decision target and transport both effects to it under the shared effect modifier assumption..
    Cites arxiv:2510.18071: A dedicated methodological response to the MAIC paradox that fixes a single common target (the overlap population) rather than a sponsor-specific one..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens
:   **partially-solved / supported-with-caveat.** C1 and C2 are technically possible: if swapping the IPD trial swaps the target population and the marginal treatment contrast varies across populations, the sign can reverse without a software error. C3 explains the constructed target-population paradox but is not the only possible cause of discordant MAICs; sampling error, different adjustment sets, model misspecification, and measurement differences can also reverse results. C4 is right for an unprincipled average of different estimands. A weighted average can be valid only if it is deliberately defined as an effect in a specified mixture population and the required linearity or standardization conditions hold. C5 states the correct design principle, subject to common support, compatible outcome definitions, and sufficient data or assumptions to transport both effects. C6 is acceptable as saying Jiang et al. describes the phenomenon, not that it uniquely discovered it. The conceptual cause and common-target remedy are already available; feasibility and empirical frequency remain open, so very-high severity is conditional rather than automatic.
    Cites doi:10.1017/rsm.2025.10: Demonstrates and explains the reversal as comparison of population-specific estimands rather than necessarily a software contradiction..
    Cites doi:10.1177/0272989X17725740: Already prescribes choosing the decision target and transporting effects to it under stated assumptions..
    Cites arxiv:2510.18071: Implements a common overlap-population target as one concrete response to sponsor-specific target reversal..

Decision path
:   `R3:partially-solved(n=2) → R11:caveated(n=2)`
